After spending a good amount of time on a utxo accumulator in an attempt to parallelize confirmations, I've come to the conclusion that this is not really possible. The accumulation must be performed sequentially to be useful, even if it's performed in parallel by block and then rolled up - the roll up is at best log(n) by splitting sets of blocks into halves and rolling up. But each division increases the cost of the roll-up accordingly, so it amounts to the same. It's still linear in the chain to accumulate the outputs. And the accumulation is only useful at its current height, requiring all previous blocks accumulated.

So if you have a milestone/checkpoint segment, you need to roll all of that up as well. That can take as long as the sync itself, or longer, just to obtain the previous outputs. I tested this by just querying to obtain the inputs and their previous outputs by
uint64_t

primary key (not hash IDs). Just querying to obtain all of these takes almost 2 hours on a machine where the sync take 50 minutes. The big part of this cost is associating the prevouts, since they are pointed to by the inputs points, which are natural keys
[hash:index]

. This is necessary due (1) download concurrency, and (2) write-only tables - which are why the sync is fast.

We pay this cost once already, during validation, to obtain the prevouts for validation. Any implementation needs to do this - to search for the hashes to match up inputs to prevouts. But to perform confirmation we are doing it a second time (for the blocks that are not checkpoint/milestone, the ones we validate). So the idea of accumulation was that we could accumulate in the same (validation) stage, and roll up out of order. However that requires significant additional work for milestone/checkpoint runs in order to fully populate the accumulator. It also then requires total ordering, as described above...

So I decided that our method of confirming only blocks that we are validating is probably optimal, yet we need a way to reduce this prevout association cost. This is a hashmap search of each input point (32 byte hash), and a hashmap search of each of these hashes in the tx table, in order to obtain a link to the puts table entry which provides the list of outputs. The links are very fast, but big table hashmap searches are much more expensive, and we avoid them during sync to prevent thrashing.

To put it in context, there are 1.03 billion entries in the tx table, and 2.6 billion entries in the input point table (unless compressed but that requires search during sync). This means that we are searching through the entire 2.6 billion entry table and 1.03 billion entry table, 2.6 billion times each. That's 5.2 billion hashmap searches performed during validation, and again during confirmation, if we are validating/confirming the full chain. That's
10.4 billion
hashmap searches just to associate all of the previous outputs. It's very fast considering, but can be much better.

elements.text:
So I'm planning to use some disk space for optimization of this expensive navigation. During validation, when validated prevouts are necessarily navigated, we can obtain the full set of output primary keys in order, for the given block.

We can then store these in an array table contiguously (5 bytes each). The offset to the start of this set is an array index in the table, which is also 5 bytes, since there's one element for each of 2.6 billion inputs (ceiling(log2(2.8b)) = 32 and one more byte is required for growth). This implies a main table of 12.2GiB to hold the prevout primary keys in groups by block.

Since blocks are validated out of order, which is where we obtain this set, we write the set in the validation chaser. The sets are written out of order and require an ordered index. We don't want to be searching for them, as that's the original problem. So we don't simply append to a hash table using the block primary key. Instead we bend one of our rules and then compensate for it.

The prevout table is an array with a trivial (empty) head. We then provide a small array index, very much like the candidate and confirmed indexes, where the entry in the index is the prevout table PK for the block, and the array offset of the index is the candidate block height. This provides direct navigation from the block height to the set of prevout (output) primary keys. From this there is also direct navigation to the tx and direct access to the output index, value, and script. We can then search the tx PK in the strong_tx table for ordered confirmedness.

However we also need to know which of the outputs are of the coinbase. These will always be first, but the count must be known, since a CB can have any number of outputs. Instead of marking every one of billions of entries with a 1 byte boolean (2.4GiB) we add the a byte count to the index entry (2.4 MiB). We could also merge a 1 bit flag into every output PK, which would be free apart from trivial processing.

But we also need the height and mtp of the prevout.tx.header (prevout's block) so that we can perform maturity checks (coinbase maturity and bip68 relative locktime). We could possibly perform these during validation, though that requires some denormalization, since these take a dependency on the prevout's tx/block, which are not referenced in validation. This can be resolved by storing the header PK (3 bytes) with the prevout PK. This bumps us up from 12.2GiB to 19.4GiB, so not trivial. This could be optimized out by the denormalization. Also the coinbase outputs can be derived from the block's first tx, but that's more costly than saving the bits is worth. The minimum cost for the scheme is about 12.2GiB.

So we start with the normal form at 19.4GiB and optimize down to 12.2GiB, and have search-free access to all prevouts and required metadata for confirmation.

For every block we validate, we confirm that each prevout is in a candidate block by chasing the prevout.tx->strong_tx. If the strong_tx is not found there is a possibility of a duplicate tx having been stored, one for the strong candidate block and one discovered in the validation search. In this case the full set of txs with that hash much be search. This is extremely rare but must be covered (never happens in pure uninterrupted block sync/validation but may happen with unconfirmed txs, reorganizations, or disk full stops).

elements.text: The bending of the rules pertains to append-only table bodies. There is already a slight bend to this in the case of the two height indexes (simple arrays), as we allow the arrays to shrink during a reorg, and then grow again. In the case of a new prevouts table, the index table for the prevouts (also a simple array) must be written out of order. The height indexes are pure stacks (push/pop only). The block order is dictated by the order of block validation. This technique allows the node to produce a sort of the unsorted validation order at no cost - by just inserting the prevouts reference into the table at the height offset.

I was able to simplify this confirmation caching design a lot. The tx locking (prevent duplicates while confirming) idea is out, too costly and complex, and not necessary. By merging the point table back into the spend table things also get simpler, and we save 19GB on the current store and drop a table. The only downsides are we can't optionally reduce store size by 50GB through point hash consolidation, but it's a little costly during sync, and prohibitive on small machines. Hopefully the significantly increased size of the spend table wouldn't create a new paging issue, but I don't think so. It's less data and fewer queries overall. In that consolidation we drop a 4 byte link and 4 byte reference for every spend, so we save 19GB total, which incidentally is the same size of the new cache. However the new cache can be dropped after validation. So this saves us an actual 19GB over the uncompressed store state, at the cost of not being able to compress out another 31GB. That puts us very close to Core store size (we were 25 GB larger or smaller depending on the consolidation option).

The cache itself becomes the id of the prevout tx (4 bytes) and the id of the spend of the prevout (4 bytes). With these two values there are no hashmap searches apart from searching for the confirming (strong) block of the tx. Basically everything is done in validation, which is parallel by block, except for this last step, which cannot be parallelized because the strong relation must be done in order by block while confirming. So I feel pretty good about the optimization being right at this point, and that it will be very effective.

elements.text: Ok, I think I figured out the best way to handle the random access index population for the prevout confirmation cache. It's really a table head, providing pointers into the array. Table heads are random access, which resolves the fault recovery question. The issue then moves to the fact that our table headers are fixed length. However I don't see this as an actual constraint. elements.text:
Our existing tables consist of a head and body, where the head stores the body size and an array of hashmap buckets. For non-hashmap tables (array or blob) the head is just a size. However this index is not a hashmap, so there's some generalization necessary.

hashmap heads are implemented using the array template. This is the same template used for array bodies. Each bucket is an offset pointer into the body, identifying the first element of the hashmap conflict list. We can generalize this array-indexed array as a hashmap with no conflicts. That requires that each valid search key has exactly one bucket. This is easy since the search key is the block height. So 850k buckets have 850k pointers into the body, and there is never a need to walk to a second element in the conflict list.

The hash function for this would be a pass-through (no-hash) of the block height. This is also something we already do, with the exception that the hash is key modulo bucket count. But in this case we don't want to modulo, we want to increase the bucket count. Bucket count is a runtime (non-template) parameter. It's defined in config and verified at startup against head size. But since it's not a template argument it's an easy change.

On verify we allow an increase (decrease still implies a fault) by just updating the bucket count member. This makes the verification a little weaker, since it trusts the increased size, but it's already weak. The check is more of a smoke check, not a true guard. So that's the first change.

On write we allow expansion of the head. Heads and bodies are implemented over the same basic mmap wrapper, which we use for this type of expansion in the bodies. However since it never happens in the heads (until now) the remap shared pointer is not necessary, as there is no reason to block global access during a remap. So in this case the remap guards must be in place, especially since writes will be concurrent (coming from the validation stage) as will reads (coming non-concurrently but concurrent with writes). So that's the second change.

When we remap we always over allocate, because remap is expensive. Heads are small, and this is with small growth, but still do not want to grow as slow as one word at a time (default behavior would be more random than that due to out of order writes at different heights). So we will have to truncate to logical size on close, which we also do for bodies but may not for heads - not sure. So that's a third thing.

snapshot/restore/disk-full are not affected. start/stop are not affected.

The treatment of it as a specialized hashmap has one more implication. The link size (in this case 3 bytes due to the number of elements we need to index - block height) is used in the as the bucket element size, and also the single word logical body size stored in the header. In the templates this is also used for the conflict linked list pointers. That would result in each array element having an extra three bytes to hold an unnecessary null pointer. So there is an issue here where we need zero length links and 3 byte keys. I believe these are the same templatized size/type. That might be enough to cause it to become an array-indexed array, as opposed to a full hashmap. This is the fourth thing, and first to verify.

That's it, just some implementation details for a single table. The table is a cache (disposable validation data), not archive (primary data). I think I'd name it
prevout

elements.text: I've also looked into a design issue pertaining to neutrino filters. Way back during table design I settled on a consolidated neutrino filters table, for the filter and filer head. These can be computed at the same time, but the filter can be computed at validation time (concurrently, partial block order) and the head must be computed from the previous head (total block order). Because this filter requires the full block and prevouts it only makes sense to compute it during validation, but the head cannot be computed until confirmation. So I'm adding a
neutrino_head
table (simple height-based array) and renaming the other to
neutrino_filter
. This will then be a complete/functional feature.

Because this filter requires the full block and prevouts it only makes sense to compute it during validation, but the head cannot be computed until confirmation. So I'm adding a `neutrino_head` table (simple height-based array) and renaming the other to `neutrino_filter`. This will then be a complete/functional feature.

elements.text:
I've just merged the changes to write the prevout cache for validated blocks. Only the prevout parent tx primary key and its coinbase-ness are written, and I've merged the coinbase bit into the 32 bit tx pk word (enough space for like 8 more years). I'm not sure that writing the spend pk will be necessary, but that can be quickly added.

The writes are bypassed for block-internal spends, as these spends are confirmable as long as they pass relative locktime checks, which require no chain context apart for bip68 activation. So this is checked during populate for validation. This saves about 9% of "is-confirmed" confirmation calls. No space is saved because I'm using a sentinel value to maintain prevout positions within the block. This eliminates the need for storing a count, and provides an easy correlation to spends that do not need to be checked for "is-not-double-spending", saving 9% of those confirmation calls as well.

I spend a good part of the day isolating a problem that turned out to be that I needed to check for bip68 activation before applying the relative locktime checks in populate. That's now merged and I'm running a performance test to get the performance cost of the additional writes (and relative locktime checks, which should be trivial).

Next is to adapt the confirmable query by incorporating the prevout cache, and then measure the performance change on the maxi/mini machines.

I've fully resolved the issue with the default custom allocator and now have complete runs with both the linear allocator and the default allocator. Issue was lack of deleter invocation in the non-detachable allocator scenario (which only affected use with the default allocator). Performance is similar, with the linear allocator slightly outperforming. Note that the power of the linear allocator is that incoming blocks may be fed across threads without causing a deallocation storm (major performance hit).

This was unrelated to the issue I was dealing with the other day, but I felt it was important to finally figure out what was wrong with the default allocator, since they appeared to be related issues. So everything looking excellent again, trivial fixes in both cases, and some other improvements along the way. Now back to optimizing confirmation.
